transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-11
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~43 minutes
Location: Zoom / Fireflies capture
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Evan Kline (Quantawell CTO), Maya Ortiz (Quantawell ML), Liam Ford (Quantawell SRE)

Optional auto sections (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Summary: Quick mid-pilot checkpoint to compare Redwood bench numbers to Quantawell's incumbent provider. Reviewed latency 95/99, p50, throughput curves, and unit cost delta. Discussed steady-state run and get raw logs for reproducibility. Agreed on follow-ups: steady-state load, security docs, and more prompt samples for regression.
Topics: benchmark delta vs incumbent, tail latency sources, batch sizing & kv-cache behavior, quantization impact, cost math, security/SSO question.
Action items: see action_items field (below).
Questions: how reproducible are the delta numbers, what causes the 99th tail spikes, can we route with fallback to cheaper variant, how will dedicated slots affect price?

Transcript body:
00:00 Sofia (Redwood): All right everyone, thanks for joining, we'll give folks a minute to hop on. Hey Evan, Maya, Liam — can you hear me okay?
00:08 Evan (Quantawell): Yep, loud and clear. Thanks.
00:12 Marcus (Redwood SE): Hi all — Marcus here, I'll run through the bench artifacts and the lab configs we used then dig into the 95/99s. Quick note: some of the filenames in the spreadsheet have slight typos, so follow the link Sofia sent.
00:26 Maya (Quantawell): Got it. We pulled the sheet, saw the latency columns, some questions already.
00:34 Sofia: Cool. Goal for today: share the annotated benchmark, explain root causes for tail spikes vs your incumbent, agree on a steady-state run, and align next steps. Does that sound right?
00:42 Evan: Yes, and also we want a clear cost delta — if your p99 is better but cost is way higher it's a problem.
00:50 Marcus: Totally. Opening the bench summary: p50, p95, p99 for our Redwood-hosted run on the quantized 13B variant, sequence length 256 typical, concurrency sweeps 1–64.
01:05 Marcus: Quick caveat — the lab used simulated traffic derived from the sample prompts you gave; we noticed a heavier prefix reuse so caching helped. If production traffic has less prefix repetition the savings will be less.
01:25 Liam (Quantawell): That's a good flag. Our prod traffic has a lot of unique prompts per session, less repetition than the test harness.
01:33 Marcus: Noted. So headline numbers: baseline vendor (your incumbent) p50 42ms, p95 180ms, p99 420ms under their 32-concurrency test. Our Redwood-hosted run showed p50 38ms, p95 150ms, p99 310ms at comparable concurrency — so better tail in our runs.
01:56 Maya: Huh okay that's promising, but why the discrepancy at p99 — any idea?
02:02 Marcus: Two big contributors: quantization kernel characteristics and KV cache eviction patterns. In our bench we used an int8 hybrid quant profile; in some cases the kernel falls back to slower fp32 path for long sequences or when attention dims are different, which creates spikes. Also when prefix reuse isn't present our internal cache evicts more often causing occasional recompute of KV that costs time on the critical path.
02:31 Evan: Are those fallback cases something you can control? Like pin a kernel so it doesn't fall back mid-run?
02:36 Marcus: There are levers. We can pin a specific kernel selection and add a TTL to the KV cache or increase reserved cache memory in Dedicated. Both reduce tail latency but might slightly increase baseline cost.
02:49 Sofia: Quick commercial note — Dedicated slots let you assign reserved GPU memory and avoid noisy neighbor effects; price changes but the latency is more predictable.
02:58 Evan: We're interested in Dedicated if the unit economics are right. How big a delta are we talking cost-wise?
03:05 Marcus: On our preliminary calc in the spreadsheet we attached, under your throughput profile the per-1k-token cost on hosted with caching is roughly 0.9x of incumbent for the quantized variant, but if you go Dedicated and reduce p99 tail we see about 1.1x cost (higher) but p99 drops by ~15–25%. I'll send the full calc.
03:24 Maya: That's helpful. Can you link the raw logs? We want to sanity-check the histograms and see the outliers with stack traces or at least timestamps.
03:31 Sofia: Yep, link is in the meeting notes — "redwood/qw/bench-raw-20270311" — Marcus, confirm that's the right bucket.
03:36 Marcus: Confirmed. There's also a separate trace file where we sampled 99th events with a rough stack (some microsecond-level kernel traces, may be noisy).
03:47 Liam: One operational question: our security team will want to know data retention, SSO, and whether you support bringing keys (KMS/HSM) in Private. We briefly saw the doc but need an engineer call.
03:58 Sofia: Absolutely — we'll do a security deep-dive next week. I'll bring our security engineer in the sync. That was one of the next steps.
04:06 Evan: Back to latency — can you explain the throughput curves? At concurrency 32, Redwood throughput flatlines — is that because of batching thresholds?
04:16 Marcus: Yes, the runtime uses continuous batching with an adaptive window. If you have a tight arrival pattern the windows fill and benefit from larger batches; if arrivals are bursty with many small requests you hit smaller effective batch sizes which limits throughput. It's a tradeoff: bigger batches = better cost per token, but slightly higher median latency.
04:34 Maya: In our prod we expect bursty traffic, single-request per user. That might mean we won't see the caching benefits.
04:41 Marcus: Right. For that traffic pattern, two levers we recommended in the bench: 1) smaller per-request batch target but priority on low-latency kernels; 2) use the routing policy to favor low-latency variants during peak windows, fallback to cheaper quantized model off-peak.
05:00 Evan: Does Redwood support automatic fallback to a different model in the same API call path?
05:05 Marcus: Yes, we have smart routing — you can set policies to route by latency SLO or cost. We can demo the routing rules in the next call.
05:13 Maya: Okay. A couple of nitty-gritty items I noticed in the spreadsheet — the tokenization mismatch column, some lines show 4–5 tokens difference between your token counters and ours. Could that affect the cost math?
05:24 Marcus: Tokenization differences can absolutely change the per-token bill. We used the model's native tokenizer but there are edge cases. We should align on canonical tokenizer and sample text. Action: Maya send two production prompt sets (see action items).
05:35 Evan: Looking at the p99 delta vs incumbent, is it possible the incumbent is running with a heavily pruned model or a different attention pattern that gives them advantage at p50 but bad p99?
05:48 Marcus: Possible. We tried to get exact model variants from them but only had their public config. Their p50 is comparable; their p99 rises likely due to background maintenance and their autoscaler causing cold-starts at high concurrency. We didn't see the same in our Dedicated run due to pinned workers.
06:05 Sofia: To be concrete, next experimental steps we propose: run a 1-hour steady-state at your real prompt mix on dedicated reserved slots; collect traces and histograms; then run a bursty pattern test to mirror your worst-case window. We'll share the raw logs and the quantization profile we used.
06:21 Evan: Sounds good. How soon can you run the one-hour?
06:24 Marcus: We can start the run Tuesday morning if you sign off on the exact prompt set by Monday EOD. It takes about two hours to provision dedicated slots in our lab calendar (not the customer Dedicated env).
06:38 Maya: We'll try to get those prompts to you by Monday.
06:40 Liam: Also, we need to validate that the HSM/KMS integration for Private deployment won't add network hops that push the p99 above what you showed. That could be a deal breaker.
06:52 Marcus: Good point — we can measure that by simulating a cross-zone KMS access in the steady-state run and report the delta. Usually the KMS negotiate adds a tiny auth cost but the per-token cost isn't affected much if keys are cached locally in the host.
07:07 Sofia: I'll add the security follow-up to next steps and pull in our security engineer.
07:10 Evan: One more: on the subject of quantization, you said you used a hybrid int8; did that require any tokenizer changes or was it transparent?
07:19 Marcus: Transparent at the API level. The runtime maps to quant kernels, but we did notice some tokens triggered slower attention paths — again tied to kernel fallbacks. We're going to try a different quant profile (more conservative) in the steady-state run to see if p99 improves while cheaps the overall cost.
07:36 Maya: Any indication on throughput per GPU in Dedicated for your 13B quantized variant? Our incumbent advertises 800 tokens/sec per card.
07:45 Marcus: In our lab Dedicated numbers, single GPU sustained ~920 tokens/sec at steady batch size for the 13B quantized with our optimized kernels. But remember this is sensitive to sequence length and batch strategy. If your average seq len is 320 instead of 256 that number drops ~12–18%.
08:05 Evan: Okay, so not a massive gap.
08:09 Sofia: Going to open the shared sheet now — (link) redwood/share/qw/bench-summary. We annotated a few rows where p99 events came from kernel fallback.
08:21 Maya: I'm scanning... I see one trace at timestamp 12:34:07 where there is a 1.2s spike — is that noise from the VM or a kernel fallback?
08:30 Marcus: That's one of the kernel fallback events; you can see the stack sample has a slow memcpy then a fallback to a different GEMM implementation. We'll attach that microtrace.
08:41 Evan: Does your runtime do any pre-warm to avoid those memcpys?
08:45 Marcus: We do pre-warm heuristics, but in the hosted runs the scheduler sometimes reclaims memory under heavy churn. In Dedicated you can pin memory and avoid that.
08:55 Liam: For the steady-state test, can you produce an artifact showing GPU utilization, memory pressure, and per-thread latency so our infra team can poke at it?
09:05 Marcus: Yes — we'll include per-GPU perf counters, host-level metrics, and the microtraces.
09:12 Evan: About cost math: your sheet shows a per-1k-token cost advantage on hosted but Dedicated is higher. Is there a middle ground like dedicated burst slots?
09:23 Marcus: We do offer burst capacity on top of reserved as an add-on — you keep baseline reserved for steady throughput and burst into pooled capacity. Pricing model is in the deck Sofia will send. That can let you hit lower tails during surge without permanently paying for reserved capacity.
09:40 Maya: That could be interesting.
09:42 Sofia: Quick checkpoint — we've hit about 10 minutes of Q&A, want to make sure we allocate time for the steady-state plan and responsibilities. Any urgent items we missed?
09:51 Evan: Nothing else from my side.
09:54 Maya: No.
09:56 Sofia: Okay. Recap then: Marcus will run 1-hour steady-state on Tuesday once Maya sends prompts; Sofia will send consolidated spreadsheet and pricing deck by Friday (or earlier); security sync week of 2027-03-22; Quantawell to confirm whether they want Dedicated pilot or prefer hosted extended pilot after seeing steady-state.
10:17 Liam: Quick nit — can you label the raw logs with run-id and seed so we can match to our ingestion pipeline?
10:23 Marcus: Will do, we'll prefix filenames with qw-run-YYYYMMDD-runid.
10:28 Sofia: Anything else?
10:31 Evan: No, that's it. Thanks.
10:33 Sofia: Thank you all — we'll follow up via email with the artifacts and schedule.

(End of call capture)
